findings.truth: The board must not be named in student-facing text, and 'Food Technology' is the retired pre-2016 qualification. This course is Food Preparation and Nutrition.

findings.truth: Same problem: the board is named and the qualification name is wrong.

findings.claim: When answering AQA questions about vitamins…
findings.truth: The board must not be named in student-facing text.
findings.evidence: house rule on board naming

findings.claim: For your AQA exam, you need to know six minerals…
findings.truth: The board must not be named in student-facing text. The six minerals themselves are right.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.2.2 (calcium, iron, sodium, fluoride, iodine, phosphorus)

findings.claim: In AQA Food Technology, “explain” questions about minerals…
findings.truth: The board is named and the qualification name is wrong.
findings.evidence: spec title page; house rule on board naming

findings.claim: Many areas in the UK add fluoride to the water supply specifically to reduce tooth decay.
findings.truth: About 6 million people, roughly one in ten of the UK population, receive artificially fluoridated water. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have no schemes at all.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Water fluoridation in the United Kingdom (fetched 18 Sep 2026)

findings.claim: Flashcard answer reads '60ndash75'.
findings.truth: The answer should read 60–75%. An HTML entity was flattened into the plain-text field, so the card shows broken text to the student.
findings.evidence: lesson body: 'typically 60–75% of total energy expenditure'

findings.claim: reference intakes = 'The daily amount of a nutrient that is enough to meet the needs of most people in a particular group.'
findings.truth: That is the definition of the reference nutrient intake (RNI). A reference intake is the guideline daily amount of energy or a nutrient shown on a food label for an average adult (2,000 kcal). Lessons 1 and 10 define it correctly, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: lesson 1 and lesson 10 definitions; food labelling reference intakes

findings.claim: Question 6 is typed '12 marks + 4 SPaG — Extended response' and the mark scheme awards '4 marks for spelling, punctuation, grammar'.
findings.truth: This subject carries no separate SPaG marks. The written paper is 1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks, 50% of the GCSE: 20 marks of multiple choice plus five questions with sub-questions worth 80 marks. The spec never mentions spelling, punctuation or grammar marks.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Assessments; full-text search of the spec for 'spelling'/'SPaG' returns nothing

findings.claim: Question 6 is typed '12 marks + 4 SPaG — Extended' with a 4-mark spelling and grammar line.
findings.truth: Same error: no SPaG marks exist in this subject.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Assessments

findings.claim: You need to know six key pathogens for the exam.
findings.truth: The spec names five food-poisoning bacteria: campylobacter, e-coli, salmonella, listeria and staphylococcus aureus. Clostridium perfringens is extra, useful but not required.
findings.evidence: spec 3.4.1.4 Bacterial contamination

findings.claim: binary fission = 'The rapid increase in bacterial numbers that occurs when conditions are favourable…'
findings.truth: Binary fission is the process itself: one bacterial cell splits into two identical cells. The wording given describes the resulting growth, not the mechanism.
findings.evidence: standard microbiology definition

findings.claim: When AQA asks you to “explain”… lifts your answer from Level 1 to Level 2.
findings.truth: 'Level 1' and 'Level 2' are banned mark-scheme band names and the board is named. Use house band vocabulary instead.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned-string list

findings.claim: Green = salad & vegetables… Brown = raw vegetables & fruit (and 'green = veg… brown = fruit' in the takeaways).
findings.truth: In the six-board colour system green is salad and fruit, and brown is vegetables. The lesson has the two swapped, and the takeaway contradicts the key-fact box in the body.
findings.evidence: standard UK colour-coded chopping board system (red raw meat, blue raw fish, yellow cooked meat, green salad and fruit, brown vegetables, white bakery and dairy)

findings.claim: The three medical conditions you must know for AQA are coeliac disease, lactose intolerance and nut allergy.
findings.truth: The board is named, and the spec sets two intolerances (gluten and lactose) plus six allergies: nuts, egg, milk, wheat, fish and shellfish. Telling students only three are needed understates the examinable content.
findings.evidence: spec 3.5.1.2 Food choices

findings.claim: Questions on food science are common in Section B of the AQA Food Preparation and Nutrition exam.
findings.truth: There is no Section B. The paper is 20 marks of multiple choice plus five questions with sub-questions worth 80 marks. Section codes are also banned wording.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Assessments

findings.claim: Mark schemes for questions 5 and 6 read 'award marks across Level 1–3'.
findings.truth: 'Level 1'–'Level 9' band names are banned. The band labels used lower down the same schemes (Top band / Mid band / Lower band) are the house wording.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned-string list

findings.claim: In AQA Food Preparation and Nutrition, questions about food provenance…
findings.truth: The board must not be named in student-facing text.
findings.evidence: house rule on board naming

findings.claim: Mark schemes for questions 5 and 6 read 'award marks across Level 1–3'.
findings.truth: Banned band names, as F17.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned-string list

findings.claim: 'Margarine and spreads must contain added vitamins A and D', repeated in the key fact, and knowledge check 4 asks 'Which nutrients must be added to margarine and spreads by UK law?'
findings.truth: Fortification of margarine with vitamins A and D is no longer mandatory in the UK; the requirement was revoked and brought into line with other spreads. Manufacturers still add them voluntarily. The spec itself only lists 'vitamins A and D added to fats and low fat spreads' as an example of fortification, never as a legal duty. The four nutrients required in white flour (thiamin, niacin, calcium, iron) are correct and untouched.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Margarine — 'Fortification with vitamins A and D is no longer mandatory for margarine' (fetched 18 Sep 2026); spec 3.6.2.2

findings.claim: When the AQA exam asks you to describe a cuisine…
findings.truth: The board must not be named in student-facing text.
findings.evidence: house rule on board naming

findings.truth: Banned band names, as F17.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned-string list

findings.claim: Every year in the UK, around one million people suffer from foodborne illness.
findings.truth: One million matches the Food Standards Agency's 2012 estimate. A later FSA estimate puts UK foodborne disease far higher (of the order of 2.4 million cases a year). I could not reach the FSA page to confirm the current figure, so I have not changed it. Options: leave the 2012 figure, or replace it once the current FSA estimate is verified. Recommendation: update to the current FSA figure after one confirming fetch.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Foodborne illness, citing the FSA 2012 report; FSA pages returned 404/410 on fetch

findings.claim: The 48-hour rule … This is a legal requirement under food safety regulations.
findings.truth: Food hygiene law requires a food business to keep anyone with diarrhoea or vomiting away from food handling, but the 48-hour figure itself comes from Food Standards Agency fitness-to-work guidance, not from a stated figure in the regulations. Most GCSE textbooks call it a legal requirement. Recommendation: soften to 'food safety law requires this, and the official guidance sets the wait at 48 hours' if Tom wants strict accuracy; otherwise leave, because it matches taught convention.
findings.evidence: FSA Food Handlers: Fitness to Work guidance; Regulation 852/2004 Annex II Chapter VIII

findings.claim: The Eatwell Guide is attributed to Public Health England.
findings.truth: Public Health England was abolished in 2021; the guide now sits with the Department of Health and Social Care. The attribution is historically right for the 2016 publication, so no edit made.
findings.evidence: general knowledge of the PHE abolition

findings.claim: Five descriptions run over the 100-character validator limit: L5 (111), L9 (100), L11 (105), L12 (110), L13 (107).
findings.truth: Not a fact error, so not edited here, but the unit will trip the description-length check if it is ever revalidated.
findings.evidence: measured from the raw dumps

findings.claim: Eight essential amino acids, with histidine listed as conditionally essential in young children.
findings.truth: Modern nutrition counts nine essential amino acids, including histidine for adults. The eight-plus-conditional framing is the standard GCSE Food convention and matches mark schemes, so it is left alone.
findings.evidence: standard GCSE Food teaching vs current nutrition science

findings.claim: Dietary fibre is called non-starch polysaccharide (NSP) while quoting the 30 g a day target.
findings.truth: The 30 g target uses the newer AOAC definition of fibre; the older NSP measure carried an 18 g target. Both labels appear in current textbooks. The 30 g figure itself is right.
findings.evidence: SACN Carbohydrates and Health, 2015

findings.claim: Most food-poisoning bacteria are aerobic (they need oxygen).
findings.truth: Most of the named pathogens are facultative anaerobes: they grow with or without oxygen. The claim is a common textbook simplification and the practical advice around it is sound.
findings.evidence: standard microbiology

findings.claim: The mandatory nutrition panel shows values per 100g and per serving.
findings.truth: Only the per 100 g or per 100 ml declaration is mandatory; per portion is voluntary extra information. Everything else in the mandatory list is correct.
findings.evidence: food labelling rules on the nutrition declaration

findings.claim: UK law requires white flour to be fortified with thiamin, niacin, calcium and iron.
findings.truth: Correct as it stands. The government has announced that folic acid will be added to non-wholemeal wheat flour, but the regulations are still under a four-nation review, so the list of four is current. Worth revisiting when the amendment comes into force.
findings.evidence: gov.uk announcement on folic acid in flour (fetched 18 Sep 2026)

findings.claim: Broken fragments left by an earlier automated edit: 'For the exam , you need…' in lessons 9 and 10, and 'You must be able to list these For the exam .' in lesson 10.
findings.truth: A stray space before the comma or full stop and a capital F mid-sentence. Text damage, not a fact error, so outside this pass; worth a tidy-up pass on the unit.
findings.evidence: raw dumps of lessons 9 and 10

summary: All 13 lessons carry at least one finding. The nutrition science is sound: kcal values, RNIs, the 5%/11%/35%/50% energy targets, 30 g fibre, 6 g salt, 6–8 glasses, the 14 allergens, the danger zone and the core temperatures all check out against the spec and government guidance, and every knowledge-check answer key is correct. The real damage is in the exam framing: two lessons invent 4 SPaG marks this subject does not award, one invents a Section B, four name the board (three of them under the retired 'Food Technology' name), and six mark schemes use banned band-name wording. Two legal or scope claims are wrong: margarine fortification is no longer mandatory, and the spec sets five food-poisoning bacteria and eight dietary conditions rather than six and three. Two definitions (reference intakes, binary fission) describe something else, one flashcard answer is entity-corrupted, and the six-board chopping-board colours are swapped.
